Also in 1903, Mann abandoned his naturalistic style, which he considered \"mechanical\" and published two  novellas, \"Tonio Kroger\" and Tristan\" in another style, which he considered \"musical\".  As a  consequence, he was now popular both with the public that liked \"Buddenbrooks\" and with the intellectuals who liked the novellas.  In 1905, Mann married a woman he had been pursuing for two years -- Katja, the daughter of Pringsheim,  Professor of Mathematics at Munich University. In 1911, after a holiday in Venice was cut short by a cholera outbreak, and during which he had been fascinated by a beautiful young Polish boy in his hotel, Mann wrote about this experience in a novel that gained great popularity, \"Death in Venice,\"  serialised in 1912, and appearing as a book in 1913. In 1914, Mann began writing \"The Magic Mountain\", not published until 1924. After the publication of \"The Magic Mountain\",  Mann wrote the novellas \"Early Sorrow\" and \"Mario and the Magician\".  As the  political situation darkened in Europe, Mann's essays stressed the importance of tolerance, warned that the humane impulse in man was in danger of being stripped away, and pointed up the need for reason to balance popular enthusiasm. In 1929, Mann was awarded the Nobel Prize for Literature. In 1930, Mann spoke out against Nazism, giving a  lecture in Berlin titled \"An Appeal to Reason\".  He called for the formation of a united front by the middle-class intelligentsia and the Socialist workers against what he labeled the inhuman intolerance and fanaticism of the Nazis. Mann continued to speak out courageously in his essays and on lecture tours in Germany and throughout Europe. In 1933, while Mann and his wife were in Switzerland, Adolf Hitler became Chancellor of Germany.  Mann was warned by his family not to return, and settled in Zurich, from where he travelled widely in Europe and the United States,  giving lectures. In 1936, Mann's German citizenship was revoked, and in the same year, the University of Bonn revoked his honorary doctorate.  In 1938, the Mann's went to the United States.  Mann first took a post at Princeton University, then moved to Southern California in 1941.  Two years earlier, he expressed his continued admiration of Goethe in \"Lotte in Weimar\" (\"The Beloved Returns\"), which told of a hypothetical meeting between an aged Goethe and a lost love from his youth. In 1943, Mann began his most political novel, \"Doctor Faustus\", an allegorical story of a composer and his music, depicting  Germany's tragic history in the 20th century.
